new_statements.quote: Dixon (1970, 1991) writes about Mbabaram (a language from the Cairns rainforest, near Cape York) that it usually stresses the first syllable that begins with a consonant, as in (25). [...] Many Cape York languages show the same characteristics as the languages in (24) and Mbabaram. We exemplify this in (26). (26) [...] Agwamin: máta 'stone', abó 'ground'; kérindja 'star', arábin 'moon'. [p. 137-138] — VIII Stress is on the first postconsonantal syllable: Agwamin (T184): No reference. [p. 248]
new_statements.citation: Goedemans, Rob W.N. 1998. Weightless segments: a phonetic and phonological study concerning the metrical irrelevance of syllable onsets. PhD dissertation, Leiden University (LOT 9). Chapter 5, pp. 137-138, example (26); Appendix D, p. 248.
new_statements.locator: pp. 137-138 (ex. 26) and p. 248 (Appendix D, category VIII); PDF pages 139-140 and 247 of the LOT text PDF
new_statements.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: opened and page images) and re-extracted the on-disk PDF with extracted text (PDF pp. 139-140 = printed 137-138; PDF p. 247 = printed 248). Printed p.137: 'Dixon (1970, 1991) writes about Mbabaram (a language from the Cairns rainforest, near Cape York) that it usually stresses the first syllable that begins with a consonant, as in (25)' and 'Many Cape York languages show the same characteristics as the languages in (24) and Mbabaram. We exemplify this in (26).' Printed p.138 ex. (26) 'Agwamin / máta stone / abó ground / kérindja star / arábin moon' with the accents exactly as reported on the page image. Printed p.248 Appendix D: 'VIII Stress is on the first postconsonantal syll…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable that begins with a consonant: consonant-initial words are stressed on the first syllable (máta, kérindja), vowel-initial words (the initial-dropped ones) on the second syllable (abó, arábin). This is onset-conditioned rather than count-based, so on the catalog's own standard (Mbabaram, Alyawarr, Lamu-Lamu) it is coded weight-sensitive; the positional restatement would be 'initial unless the word begins with a vowel, then peninitial'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Agwamin. Goedemans' own view (ch. 5) is that this pattern is a historical artefact of initial dropping (a prior shift of stress to the second syllable followed by loss of the initial CV), i.e. the onset-conditioning is diachronic in origin.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (isolated lexical items, four accent-marked words). The Agwamin forms carry no source ('No reference' in App. D); they are presented as an instance of the Mbabaram/Aranda type in which stress is on the first syllable that has an onset (first postconsonantal syllable).
new_statements.identity_note: The only stress data found are labelled 'Agwamin' (Goedemans 1998; AIATSIS Y132), whereas the catalog key wami1239/ISO wmi is 'Wamin' (AIATSIS Y133). Sutton 1976 treats them as one language ('Hereafter I refer to Wamin/Agwamin as Wamin'; per Fred Fulford 'two mutually intelligible dialects, one heavy and one light'), and Glottolog wami1239 lists Agwamin as an alternate name, so the Agwamin statement applies to wami1239 as a whole; no separate glottocode exists for Agwamin.
